course.title: CCSP — the Cloud Assurance
course.description: Secure one small cloud application across its lifecycle and govern it: shared responsibility and the law, classified data under its own key, a fenced platform, a secure build, operations and an incident, handed over control-by-control. Built for CCSP.
course.audience: Secure and govern one small cloud application as a four-person team — everyone runs the commands, pastes the proof and fills every record; the focus decides which record you lead.

roles.name: Cloud Data Security (Data Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the data record: classification, encryption, key ownership and retention.

roles.name: Platform & Infrastructure (Platform Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the platform record: the reference architecture, the network and the controls.

roles.name: Application Security (AppSec Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the application record: the secure lifecycle, the secrets and the dependencies.

roles.name: Governance & Operations (GRC Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the records that outlive the build: law, operations, the incident and handover.

tasks.title: Open the account and guard the spend
tasks.objective: Open a cloud free account, turn on MFA for the owner, and set a $1 budget alert.
definitionOfDone: The free account is open with MFA on the owner
A $1 budget alert exists
The register names the account and who owns it

steps.title: Open the account and turn owner MFA on
steps.description: The account exists with MFA on the owner, agreed as break-glass only for routine work.
steps.instruction: Create the cloud free account for the engagement and turn on MFA for the account owner before anything else.
steps.expectedOutput: The account exists with MFA on the owner, agreed as break-glass only for routine work.
instructionList: Use a shared team email, not a personal one.
Turn on MFA for the owner immediately; it is the one identity that can do anything.
Record that the owner is break-glass only; daily work is a scoped identity.
steps.whatItMeans: The account owner is the account. Securing it first, and reserving it for break-glass, is the first control of any cloud baseline.

steps.title: Write the engagement scope file
steps.description: Write the engagement scope file
steps.instruction: Write a scope file naming the application, the data it holds and the one obligation that drives the controls, and count its lines.

commands.cmd:
printf 'app: quote-api
data: customer PII + quotes
obligation: GDPR + SOC-2
region: eu-west-1
' | tee scope.txt | wc -l
commands.explain: Writes the scope and counts the lines, so the engagement opens with a written boundary.

steps.whatItMeans: The scope is the boundary every later control is judged against. Writing it first stops scope creep and names what the law cares about.

outputHighlights.label: The scope is written, one line per fact.

tasks.title: Make an MFA identity and the CLI
tasks.objective: Create a scoped identity with MFA for daily work and confirm the CLI runs as it, not the owner.
definitionOfDone: A scoped identity with MFA exists
The CLI runs as that identity
The identity is recorded in the register

steps.title: Confirm the CLI identity is scoped, not the owner
steps.description: Confirm the CLI identity is scoped, not the owner
steps.instruction: Run the identity check and confirm the caller is the scoped user, not the account owner.

commands.cmd: echo "caller: $(whoami)@cloud profile=engagement" && grep -q engagement ~/.cloud/config && echo "scoped profile active"
commands.explain: Prints the active profile and confirms it is the scoped engagement profile, not the owner.
commands.sample:
caller: analyst@cloud profile=engagement
scoped profile active

steps.expectedOutput:
caller: analyst@cloud profile=engagement
scoped profile active
steps.whatItMeans: Every command carries an identity. Confirming it is scoped, not the owner, is how you know a mistake has limits.

outputHighlights.label: Daily work runs as a scoped identity.

fixes.fix: Create a scoped user with MFA, configure a CLI profile for it, and select that profile before any work.

tasks.title: Know your team, your focus and the folder
tasks.objective: Agree who leads which record, name the application, and make the evidence folder every artifact goes in.
definitionOfDone: Each of the four focuses has a named member
The application has a name in the pattern ccsp-t<team>
The evidence folder exists with a week-0 to week-4 layout

steps.title: Pick the focus and name the application
steps.description: Four names against four focuses, and an application name the whole team uses from now on.
steps.instruction: Agree who leads Data Security, Platform, Application Security and Governance. Name the application ccsp-t and your team number.
steps.expectedOutput: Four names against four focuses, and an application name the whole team uses from now on.
steps.whatItMeans: A focus is the record a member leads and reviews, not the only work they do. Everyone runs the commands and everyone pastes output.

steps.title: Make the evidence folder
steps.description: Make the evidence folder
steps.instruction: Create the evidence folder with a subfolder for each week. Every policy, mapping and finding goes under the week it belongs to.

commands.cmd: mkdir -p ccsp-t1/week-{0,1,2,3,4} && ls ccsp-t1
commands.explain: Five week folders in one command, then reads them back. Replace t1 with your team number.

steps.expectedOutput: week-0  week-1  week-2  week-3  week-4
steps.whatItMeans: An artifact nobody can find is an artifact nobody can hash. The folder is the first custody control.

tasks.title: The shared-responsibility line
tasks.objective: For each layer of the stack, mark who secures it — the provider or the customer — for the service model in scope.
definitionOfDone: Each layer is marked provider or customer for the model in scope
At least one layer is shown moving owner between service models
The line is recorded in the architecture record

steps.title: Build the responsibility matrix
steps.description: Build the responsibility matrix
steps.instruction: Write each layer with who secures it under the service model in scope, then count the customer-owned layers.

commands.cmd:
printf 'data	customer
app	customer
runtime	provider
os	provider
network	provider
' | tee responsibility.tsv | awk -F"	" '$2=="customer"{c++} END{print c" customer-owned layers"}'
commands.explain: Writes the responsibility matrix and counts the layers the customer must secure.

steps.expectedOutput: 2 customer-owned layers
steps.whatItMeans: The shared-responsibility line is the first thing a cloud auditor asks for: it says exactly which controls are yours to run and which the provider runs.

outputHighlights.label: The layers the team must secure.

steps.title: Show a layer moving between service models
steps.description: One layer with its owner written for all three service models, showing the line moves.
steps.instruction: Pick one layer, such as the runtime, and show who owns it under IaaS versus PaaS versus SaaS.
steps.expectedOutput: One layer with its owner written for all three service models, showing the line moves.
steps.whatItMeans: The responsibility line is not fixed: moving from IaaS to SaaS hands layers to the provider. Knowing which stops a team securing what is no longer theirs, or missing what is.

handoff.note: Your section of the Architecture & Responsibility, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: The reference architecture
tasks.objective: Name every component of the application, its trust boundary, and the data that crosses each boundary.
definitionOfDone: Every component is named with its trust zone
Every boundary crossing names the data that crosses it
The architecture is recorded with its boundaries

steps.title: List the components and their trust zones
steps.description: List the components and their trust zones
steps.instruction: Write each component with its trust zone and confirm every tier is present.

commands.cmd:
printf 'edge	public
api	app
queue	app
db	private
kms	private
' | tee components.tsv | awk -F"	" '{z[$2]++} END{for (k in z) print k": "z[k]}'
commands.explain: Writes the components and counts how many sit in each trust zone.

steps.expectedOutput:
public: 1
app: 2
private: 2
steps.whatItMeans: A component with no trust zone is a component nobody is defending. The zone decides which controls apply and what may talk to it.

outputHighlights.label: The components that must never face the public zone.

handoff.note: Your section of the Architecture & Responsibility, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: The legal and compliance scope
tasks.objective: Map the obligations the application carries to a control framework, and name where the data may and may not live.
prerequisites: The control catalogue shipped with the course (controls.json)
definitionOfDone: Each obligation maps to one or more controls in the framework
The data-residency rule is stated with its jurisdiction
The mapping is recorded in the compliance register

steps.title: Map each obligation to a control
steps.description: Map each obligation to a control
steps.instruction: Read the shipped control catalogue and list the controls that satisfy the data-protection obligation.

commands.cmd: jq -r '.controls[] | select(.obligations[]? == "data-protection") | "\(.id)\t\(.title)"' controls.json
commands.explain: Selects from the catalogue the controls that satisfy the data-protection obligation.
commands.sample:
A.8.24	Use of cryptography
A.5.34	Privacy and protection of PII

steps.expectedOutput:
A.8.24	Use of cryptography
A.5.34	Privacy and protection of PII
steps.whatItMeans: An obligation with no control mapped to it is a gap a regulator will find first. The mapping is what turns a law into something the team can actually do.

outputHighlights.label: A control that satisfies the obligation.

fixes.fix: Install jq from your package manager; it is a standard command-line JSON tool.

steps.title: State the data-residency rule
steps.description: A residency rule naming the allowed region, the forbidden ones and the law that sets it.
steps.instruction: Write where the data may live and where it must not, and the jurisdiction that decides it.
steps.expectedOutput: A residency rule naming the allowed region, the forbidden ones and the law that sets it.
steps.whatItMeans: Data residency is where cloud law bites hardest: a backup replicated to the wrong region can breach the obligation before anyone notices.

handoff.note: Your section of the Legal, Risk & Compliance, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Classify the data
tasks.objective: Give every data set in the inventory a classification, and confirm nothing is left unclassified.
prerequisites: The data inventory shipped with the course (inventory.csv)
definitionOfDone: Every data set has a classification
No row is left unclassified
The classification is recorded with its handling rule

steps.title: Confirm nothing is unclassified
steps.description: Confirm nothing is unclassified
steps.instruction: Read the data inventory and count any row whose classification column is empty.

commands.cmd: awk -F, 'NR>1 && $3=="" {u++} END{print (u+0)" unclassified rows"}' inventory.csv
commands.explain: Counts inventory rows with no classification; zero is the goal.

steps.expectedOutput: 0 unclassified rows
steps.whatItMeans: An unclassified data set is one nobody knows how to protect. Classification is the control every data rule hangs off.

outputHighlights.label: Every data set is classified.

fixes.fix: Classify each empty row in the inventory — public, internal, confidential or restricted — then re-run.

steps.title: Count the restricted data that drives the controls
steps.description: Count the restricted data that drives the controls
steps.instruction: Count the rows classified restricted, since those set the strongest handling rules.

commands.cmd: awk -F, 'NR>1 && $3=="restricted" {r++} END{print (r+0)" restricted data sets"}' inventory.csv
commands.explain: Counts the restricted data sets that drive encryption and access rules.

steps.expectedOutput: 3 restricted data sets
steps.whatItMeans: The restricted rows decide the strongest controls. Counting them tells the team how much of the build is high-stakes.

handoff.note: Your section of the Data Security Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Encrypt it and lock the store
tasks.objective: Confirm the data store encrypts at rest and refuses a public grant, so classified data cannot land in the open.
prerequisites: The store configuration shipped with the course (store.json)
definitionOfDone: The store encrypts at rest, confirmed
Public access is blocked, confirmed
The protection is recorded

steps.title: Confirm encryption and no public access
steps.description: Confirm encryption and no public access
steps.instruction: Read the store configuration and confirm encryption is on and public access is blocked.

commands.cmd: jq -r '"encryption: \(.encryption.atRest)  public: \(.publicAccess)"' store.json
commands.explain: Prints whether the store encrypts at rest and whether public access is allowed.

steps.expectedOutput: encryption: aws:kms  public: blocked
steps.whatItMeans: An encrypted store that still allows a public grant is one bad policy away from a breach. The two controls together are what keep classified data in.

outputHighlights.label: Public access is off and encryption is on.

fixes.fix: Turn Block Public Access fully on and re-export the store configuration, then re-run.

handoff.note: Your section of the Data Security Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Own the key and the lifecycle
tasks.objective: Confirm the key is customer-owned with rotation on, and record the key-ownership decision and the retention rule.
prerequisites: The key configuration shipped with the course (key.json)
definitionOfDone: The key is customer-owned with rotation on
A retention and deletion rule is recorded
The key-ownership decision is recorded with the option rejected

steps.title: Confirm the key is customer-owned and rotates
steps.description: Confirm the key is customer-owned and rotates
steps.instruction: Read the key configuration and confirm the manager is the customer and rotation is on.

commands.cmd: jq -r '"manager: \(.manager)  rotation: \(.rotation)"' key.json
commands.explain: Prints who manages the key and whether rotation is enabled.

steps.expectedOutput: manager: customer  rotation: enabled
steps.whatItMeans: A customer-owned key is one you set the policy on and can rotate, disable and destroy. A provider key gives none of that control to prove.

outputHighlights.label: The key is the team’s to govern.

steps.title: Record the key-ownership decision
steps.description: A recorded decision with its reason, the option rejected and the accepted risk.
steps.instruction: With the residency and obligation in front of the team, record the key decision: a provider key, a customer-owned key, or hold-your-own-key.
steps.expectedOutput: A recorded decision with its reason, the option rejected and the accepted risk.
steps.whatItMeans: The key decision is the drafter’s to make and own. Writing the rejected option proves a choice was made, not defaulted into.

handoff.note: Your section of the Data Security Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Secure the platform
tasks.objective: Run the platform baseline against the catalogue and confirm every must-pass control passes.
prerequisites: The baseline results shipped with the course (baseline.json)
definitionOfDone: Every must-pass control is checked
Any failing control has an owner and a fix
The baseline result is recorded

steps.title: Find the failing baseline controls
steps.description: Find the failing baseline controls
steps.instruction: Read the baseline results and list any control that failed, so each gets an owner.

commands.cmd: jq -r '.checks[] | select(.result=="fail") | "\(.id)\t\(.title)"' baseline.json; echo "scan complete"
commands.explain: Lists the failing baseline checks; an empty list before "scan complete" means a clean baseline.
commands.sample:
CIS-2.1.1	Ensure logging is enabled
scan complete

steps.expectedOutput:
CIS-2.1.1	Ensure logging is enabled
scan complete
steps.whatItMeans: A baseline you never scanned is a baseline you are only hoping holds. The failing list is the work; the clean scan is the proof.

outputHighlights.label: The baseline was scanned, pass or fail recorded.

handoff.note: Your section of the Platform & Network Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Segment the network
tasks.objective: Confirm the private tier has no public route and the app tier reaches only what it must.
prerequisites: The network configuration shipped with the course (network.json)
definitionOfDone: The private tier has no public route
Each allowed flow has a reason
The segmentation is recorded

steps.title: Prove the private tier has no public route
steps.description: Prove the private tier has no public route
steps.instruction: Read the network configuration and confirm the private tier’s routes never reach the public gateway.

commands.cmd: jq -r '.tiers.private.routes[]' network.json | grep -q public && echo "LEAK: public route" || echo "private tier has no public route"
commands.explain: Checks the private tier routes for any public path; the safe result names no leak.
commands.sample: private tier has no public route

steps.expectedOutput: private tier has no public route
steps.whatItMeans: A private tier with a public route is not private. The route table, not the subnet name, is where segmentation is really enforced.

outputHighlights.label: The private tier is sealed from the internet.

fixes.fix: Remove the public route from the private tier and route egress through a controlled gateway, then re-run.

handoff.note: Your section of the Platform & Network Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Secure the application
tasks.objective: Confirm the application has no hard-coded secret and no critical dependency vulnerability before it ships.
prerequisites: The sample source and dependency manifest shipped with the course
definitionOfDone: No hard-coded secret is found in the source
No critical dependency vulnerability remains
The scans are recorded

steps.title: Scan the source for hard-coded secrets
steps.description: Scan the source for hard-coded secrets
steps.instruction: Grep the sample source for anything that looks like a key or password, and confirm none is found.

commands.cmd: grep -rniE "(secret|password|api[_-]?key)\s*=\s*[\"\x27][^\"\x27]+" src/ && echo "SECRET FOUND" || echo "no hard-coded secret"
commands.explain: Searches the source for assigned secrets; the safe result finds none.

steps.expectedOutput: no hard-coded secret
steps.whatItMeans: A secret in code is a secret in every clone, log and backup forever. Finding none before the build ships is the control.

outputHighlights.label: The source is clean of inline secrets.

fixes.fix: Move it to a secrets manager or an environment variable, rotate the exposed value, and re-run.

steps.title: Scan the dependencies for critical vulnerabilities
steps.description: Scan the dependencies for critical vulnerabilities
steps.instruction: Read the dependency scan report and count any critical finding that must be fixed before shipping.

commands.cmd: jq -r '[.vulnerabilities[] | select(.severity=="critical")] | length | "\(.) critical vulnerabilities"' scan.json
commands.explain: Counts critical dependency vulnerabilities; zero is the ship gate.

steps.expectedOutput: 0 critical vulnerabilities
steps.whatItMeans: Most breaches ride in on a known-vulnerable dependency. The critical count is the gate: zero before the application ships.

handoff.note: Your section of the Application Security Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Run security operations
tasks.objective: Confirm monitoring is on and a change goes through a recorded, reversible process.
prerequisites: The operations configuration shipped with the course (ops.json)
definitionOfDone: Monitoring and alerting are confirmed on
A change is recorded with its rollback
The operations state is recorded

steps.title: Confirm monitoring is on and alerts route
steps.description: Confirm monitoring is on and alerts route
steps.instruction: Read the operations configuration and confirm logging is on and an alert has a destination.

commands.cmd: jq -r '"logging: \(.logging)  alert: \(.alerting.destination)"' ops.json
commands.explain: Prints whether logging is on and where alerts route; a destination means they reach a human.

steps.expectedOutput: logging: enabled  alert: secops-oncall
steps.whatItMeans: Operations is where a control baseline keeps living after the build. Logging with a real alert destination is what makes it detect, not just record.

outputHighlights.label: Monitoring is on and alerts route to a human.

handoff.note: Your section of the Operations & Incident Log, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Work the incident
tasks.objective: Work a real incident the method way: one theory, one containment action, one result per row, until it is contained.
prerequisites: The alert detail shipped with the course (alert.json)
definitionOfDone: The incident is written exactly, before any action
Every step is a row: theory, the one action, the result
At least one action did not contain it and the row says so
The incident is contained and the lesson is recorded

steps.title: Write the incident exactly
steps.description: The log opens with the actor, the resource, the unauthorized action and why it is an incident, and no actio…
steps.instruction: Before any action, write what happened from the alert: the actor, the resource, the action, and why it is an incident.
steps.expectedOutput: The log opens with the actor, the resource, the unauthorized action and why it is an incident, and no action yet.
steps.whatItMeans: The method starts with the incident written down. For a cloud incident the symptom is the exact alert, not a feeling that something is off.

steps.title: Read the alert, then contain it one action per row
steps.description: Read the alert, then contain it one action per row
steps.instruction: Read the alert detail, write one containment theory, take one action, and record the result. An action that does not contain it gets its own row.

commands.cmd: jq -r '"actor: \(.actor)  action: \(.action)  resource: \(.resource)"' alert.json && echo "theory: revoke the session → contained"
commands.explain: Reads the alert facts the incident is worked from, then records the first containment theory and its result.
commands.sample:
actor: svc-quote  action: GetObject  resource: restricted-bucket
theory: revoke the session → contained

steps.expectedOutput:
actor: svc-quote  action: GetObject  resource: restricted-bucket
theory: revoke the session → contained
steps.whatItMeans: One action per row is what makes the log trustworthy: you can always say which action contained it. The same method A+ uses on hardware.

outputHighlights.label: The first containment action and its result.

fixes.symptom: Revoking the session did not contain it?
fixes.fix: Next row: rotate the service credential, one change, and re-check whether the calls stop.

handoff.note: Your section of the Operations & Incident Log, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Hand the baseline over
tasks.objective: Map every control to the evidence that proves it, list the open risks, and hash every artifact for custody.
prerequisites: Every other record of the course, filled
definitionOfDone: Every control maps to the artifact that proves it
Each open risk has an owner and a mitigation
Every artifact has a custody row with its hash

steps.title: Map every control to its evidence
steps.description: A one-page baseline where every control points at the artifact that proves it, and each open risk has an ow…
steps.instruction: Write the baseline in one page: each control across data, platform, application and operations, and the artifact in the evidence folder that proves it.
steps.expectedOutput: A one-page baseline where every control points at the artifact that proves it, and each open risk has an owner.
steps.whatItMeans: A control with no evidence is a claim. The control-to-evidence map is what an auditor and the next team both read first.

steps.title: Hash every artifact for custody
steps.description: Hash every artifact for custody
steps.instruction: Hash every file in the evidence folder so the handover carries a custody row that proves what was delivered.

commands.cmd: find ccsp-t1 -type f -exec sha256sum {} + | tee week-4/custody.txt | wc -l && echo "custody.txt written"
commands.explain: Hashes every artifact and counts them, writing the custody list for the record.

steps.expectedOutput:
19
custody.txt written
steps.whatItMeans: A hash is what lets anyone, months later, prove the control evidence in hand is the one delivered. It is the last control of the course.

outputHighlights.label: Every artifact hashed into one custody list.

steps.title: Write the Portfolio
steps.description: The repository, the case study, three resume bullets, the diagram and the skills shown, on the shared Portfolio form.
steps.instruction: Fill the Portfolio with the whole team.
instructionList: Paste the link to the team repository, e.g. https://github.com/org/capstone-team01, that holds the configuration and documents.
Write the case study in two hundred words or more: the problem, what was built, the decisions, the result.
Write three resume bullets, each an action, a tool and a measurable result, e.g. "closed 14 of 15 findings".
Name the diagram the case study refers to, then list the skills demonstrated with the evidence for each.
steps.expectedOutput: The Portfolio is filled: a repository link, a case study of two hundred words or more, three bullets, the diagram named, three or more skills with evidence.

docs.title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010: architecture description
docs.lookFor: What an architecture description must identify: stakeholders, concerns, viewpoints and the rationale for decisions.

steps.whatItMeans: The certification proves what was learned; the Portfolio proves what was built. An employer reads this form, not the pass mark.

fixes.symptom: The case-study check stays red at two hundred words
fixes.fix: Words are counted on whitespace; a line of bullet dashes or a table is one word each. Write sentences.
It has to start with https:// and hold no spaces; paste the address bar, not the repository name.

tasks.title: AI extension: explain the responsibility line
tasks.objective: Use a local AI assistant on what you built this week: explain the responsibility line, grounded and checked.

steps.title: Run a local model
steps.description: A model that runs on your own machine, offline.
steps.instruction: Pull a small local model and list it.
instructionList: Install Ollama from the official site if it is not already there.
Run the pull command for a small model.
List the installed models and confirm it is there.

commands.cmd: ollama pull llama3.2 && ollama list
commands.explain: Pulls a small model that runs offline, then lists what is installed so you can see it is ready.
commands.sample:
NAME             ID            SIZE      MODIFIED
llama3.2:latest  a80c4f17acd5  2.0 GB    2 seconds ago

flags.meaning: Downloads the model once; it then runs offline.
Prints the installed models as a table.

steps.expectedOutput:
NAME             ID            SIZE      MODIFIED
llama3.2:latest  a80c4f17acd5  2.0 GB    2 seconds ago

outputHighlights.label: your offline model, ready

steps.whatItMeans: A model on your own machine answers without sending your work to anyone. Everything after this runs offline.

docs.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
docs.lookFor: the Manage function: run AI with controls, and keep a person accountable for what it produces.

fixes.fix: Install it from the official site, then open a new terminal so the command is on the path.

fixes.symptom: The pull is slow or fails
fixes.fix: The model is two gigabytes; on a slow link pull llama3.2:1b instead and list again.

steps.title: Ground it, and check the answer
steps.description: The model answers from your record; you keep what the evidence supports.
steps.instruction: Ask the model to explain the responsibility line, then check it.
instructionList: Paste one of your own records into the prompt as the context.
Ask the model to explain or check that record for this week.
Read the answer against your evidence and keep only what is true.
steps.expectedOutput: The model answers from your record, and you keep only the parts your evidence supports.
steps.whatItMeans: A grounded answer cites your own work; an ungrounded one guesses. The human check is what makes it safe to use.

DOMAINS.label: Technical capability
DOMAINS.definition: Skills, tools, commands and exam domains proven by pasted output that held every expected token.
DOMAINS.asks: Can this member operate the tools and run the commands the job needs?
DOMAINS.evidence: A verification record per step: the output hash, the tokens matched, the attempts, and a receipt in cloud mode.

DOMAINS.label: Professional execution
DOMAINS.definition: Procedures followed to standard, steps in order, first pastes, evidence named, checks met, documents controlled, work on time.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member follow the runbook as written and deliver on the calendar?
DOMAINS.evidence: The order of verification stamps, the attempts, the file names, the Definition-of-Done checks, the control block and the cohort due dates.

DOMAINS.label: Problem solving
DOMAINS.definition: Faults logged and resolved, steps verified after a failed paste, stuck flags cleared, and the minutes from first paste to proof.
DOMAINS.asks: When something breaks, does this member find and fix it, and how long does it take?
DOMAINS.evidence: Fault, incident and triage rows with their outcome column, retries that verified, the append-only flag history and two stamps per step.

DOMAINS.label: Thought process
DOMAINS.definition: Decisions recorded against at least three options with rationale, rejected options, risk and rollback, and reasons written on change rows.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member weigh options, say why, and plan the way back?
DOMAINS.evidence: Decision blocks with the option chosen, who chose it and when, the answers to the supporting questions, and the form lifecycle.

DOMAINS.label: Architecture and design
DOMAINS.definition: Design briefs, topologies, IP plans, bills of materials, decision records and as-built documents drafted, approved and issued.
DOMAINS.asks: Can this member design a system and write it down so another team can build it?
DOMAINS.evidence: The architecture and configuration forms of the role: rows filled, checks met, approved or issued, with the decisions on them.

DOMAINS.label: Team and communication
DOMAINS.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected, peer reviews given, steps ticked for teammates, reports filed, notes written, handovers issued.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member hand work on cleanly, review others and hold their lane?
DOMAINS.evidence: The lifecycle rows with who moved what, the hand-offs and their forms, the peer review queue, the reports and the notes.

DOMAINS.label: Learning and retention
DOMAINS.definition: Skills proved on a second task, verified again a week or more later, reused in another course, and the pace month on month.
DOMAINS.asks: Is this member still learning, and keeping what was learned?
DOMAINS.evidence: The verification stamps of every skill: first and last, the tasks and courses between them, and the last two months of them.

DOMAINS.label: Professional readiness
DOMAINS.definition: The tier per record item at ten verified uses, the exam weight verified, the work-role coverage and the readiness score.
DOMAINS.asks: Can this member consistently perform at a professional level in a real work environment?
DOMAINS.evidence: Every category of the record with its verified uses across courses, the published exam weights and the work roles’ required competencies.

KPIS.label: Skills verified
KPIS.numerator: Skills with at least one step verified from pasted output.
KPIS.denominator: Skills the role practises that carry a verifiable step.
KPIS.whyMember: Each verified skill names a task where the pasted output held every expected token.
KPIS.whyCompany: Skills backed by matched output rather than a tick, with the task behind each one named.

KPIS.label: Exam weight verified
KPIS.numerator: The published exam weight of every domain with a verified step, summed.
KPIS.denominator: The published exam weight of every domain the role practises, summed.
KPIS.whyMember: Shows which share of the exam blueprint the verified work already touches.
KPIS.whyCompany: Reads the verified work against the published exam domains and their weights.

KPIS.label: Commands verified
KPIS.numerator: Verified required steps that run a command.
KPIS.denominator: Verifiable required steps that run a command.
KPIS.whyMember: Command steps proven by their output; the table below splits them by tool.
KPIS.whyCompany: Tool use proven by output, per command step, split by tool in the table.

KPIS.label: Procedures to standard
KPIS.numerator: Followed procedures whose form cites a control code and was approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Procedures followed: every check due met and document control complete.
KPIS.whyMember: A runbook followed to a named control and approved by the team; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Procedures run to a cited NIST, ISO or SOC 2 control and approved by the team.

KPIS.label: Faults resolved
KPIS.numerator: Fault, incident and triage rows whose outcome column reads resolved.
KPIS.denominator: Fault, incident and triage rows the team filled on the forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Every fault the team logged, and how many ended resolved; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Troubleshooting success read from the fault and incident records the team kept.

KPIS.label: Verified after retry
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps that took more than one paste.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps.
KPIS.whyMember: A step that failed once and was then proven: the fault was found and fixed.
KPIS.whyCompany: How often a failed first paste was followed by a verified fix.

KPIS.label: Stuck flags cleared
KPIS.numerator: Stuck flags the member raised and later cleared.
KPIS.denominator: Stuck flags the member raised.
KPIS.whyMember: Asking for help and then getting past it both count; a flag never cleared says so.
KPIS.whyCompany: Blockers raised and worked through, from the append-only flag history.

KPIS.label: Time to resolution
KPIS.numerator: The median minutes from the first paste to the verification, per verified step with both stamps.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps with both stamps; the share within the hour is the percentage.
KPIS.whyMember: The median, so one long gap moves nothing; a step left over a day is counted apart.
KPIS.whyCompany: Minutes from first attempt to proof, read from two recorded stamps, never a clock.

KPIS.label: Steps verified in order
KPIS.numerator: Tasks whose verifiable steps were verified in the authored order.
KPIS.denominator: Tasks with two or more verification records, so an order exists.
KPIS.whyMember: The procedure was run as written, step after step.
KPIS.whyCompany: Runbooks followed in order, read from the sequence of verification records.

KPIS.label: First-try verifications
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps whose first paste held every expected token.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps.
KPIS.whyMember: Shown beside retries: a step verified after several pastes counts for as much.
KPIS.whyCompany: How often the first paste matched, printed beside how often it took more than one.

KPIS.label: Files named to convention
KPIS.numerator: Hashed files named to the evidence convention.
KPIS.denominator: Hashed files.
KPIS.whyMember: Evidence an auditor can find: date, team, tool and subject in every file name.
KPIS.whyCompany: Chain-of-custody hygiene: hashed files that follow the naming convention.

KPIS.label: Definition-of-Done met
KPIS.numerator: Definition-of-Done checks met on the forms of the role.
KPIS.denominator: Checks due on those forms through the current week.
KPIS.whyMember: Every check a form must pass this week, met or not, counted for the team.
KPIS.whyCompany: Work products measured against their own acceptance checks, week by week.

KPIS.label: Decisions recorded
KPIS.numerator: Decision blocks with an option chosen by this member.
KPIS.denominator: Decision blocks on the forms of the role, each with at least three options.
KPIS.whyMember: Each decision names the options weighed, the one chosen, who chose and when.
KPIS.whyCompany: Component, configuration and architecture choices made against named alternatives.

KPIS.label: Decisions justified
KPIS.numerator: Recorded decisions with every required supporting question answered.
KPIS.denominator: Decisions recorded by this member.
KPIS.whyMember: A choice with its reason, the rejected options and the risk accepted.
KPIS.whyCompany: Judgment shown in writing: rationale, rejected options, risk and rollback per decision.

KPIS.label: Decisions approved
KPIS.numerator: Recorded decisions on a form the team approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Decisions recorded by this member.
KPIS.whyMember: The team stood behind the choice; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Decisions that passed the team’s review and were issued.

KPIS.label: Changes with rollback
KPIS.numerator: Change-record rows with a rollback or back-out written.
KPIS.denominator: Change-record rows on the forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Every change the team logged, and how many had a way back written down first.
KPIS.whyCompany: Change discipline: a rollback plan on every recorded change.

KPIS.label: Hand-offs completed
KPIS.numerator: Hand-offs whose named deliverable reached approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Hand-offs of the tasks of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Work handed to another role that the team then approved or issued.
KPIS.whyCompany: Cross-role hand-offs closed by an approved document.

KPIS.label: RACI respected
KPIS.numerator: Lifecycle moves the member made in the role the RACI names for that move.
KPIS.denominator: Lifecycle moves the member made on forms with a RACI.
KPIS.whyMember: Submitting as the drafter, approving as the approver: the lane was held.
KPIS.whyCompany: Role discipline on documents, read from who moved what.

KPIS.label: Peer reviews given
KPIS.numerator: Blind peer reviews the member completed.
KPIS.denominator: Peer reviews assigned to the member.
KPIS.whyMember: Reviews of other teams’ frozen work, answered question by question.
KPIS.whyCompany: Review work done for others, from the blind review queue.

KPIS.label: Teammate steps ticked
KPIS.numerator: Required steps the member ticked on another role’s tasks.
KPIS.denominator: No denominator: a count.
KPIS.whyMember: Steps done on a teammate’s task, so a lane short of hands still finished.
KPIS.whyCompany: Help given across roles, counted in steps.

KPIS.label: On time
KPIS.numerator: Tasks whose last verification fell on or before the week due date.
KPIS.denominator: Tasks with a verification; needs the cohort start date.
KPIS.whyMember: The due date comes from the cohort calendar; without one the row says so.
KPIS.whyCompany: Reliability against a calendar, read from the verification stamps and the cohort start.

KPIS.label: Document control complete
KPIS.numerator: Forms with data whose document-control block is complete.
KPIS.denominator: Forms of the role with data.
KPIS.whyMember: Id, version, owner, date and status on every document the team filled.
KPIS.whyCompany: Document control kept on every filled form: id, version, owner, date, status.

KPIS.label: Controls cited
KPIS.numerator: Distinct control codes on approved or issued forms the role drafts.
KPIS.denominator: Distinct control codes the forms of the role cite.
KPIS.whyMember: The published controls the approved documents cite, by code.
KPIS.whyCompany: Control codes practised through approved documents, by standard.

KPIS.label: Instructor approved
KPIS.numerator: Forms of the role whose latest instructor review is approved.
KPIS.denominator: Forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Forms an instructor reviewed and approved; the latest review per form counts.
KPIS.whyCompany: Forms with an instructor verdict of approved, the latest review per form.

KPIS.label: Skills proved twice
KPIS.numerator: Skills with verified steps on two or more distinct tasks.
KPIS.denominator: Skills with at least one verified step.
KPIS.whyMember: A skill verified on two different tasks was carried from one context to another.
KPIS.whyCompany: Verification repeated on a second task is harder to reach by luck or by copying.

KPIS.label: Skills retained
KPIS.numerator: Skills verified again seven or more days after their first verification.
KPIS.denominator: Skills with at least one verified step.
KPIS.whyMember: Proof a week or more apart: the skill stayed.
KPIS.whyCompany: Retention read from the gap between two verification stamps on the same skill.

KPIS.label: Learning velocity
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before the page clock.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before those; the percentage caps at one hundred.
KPIS.whyMember: This month against last: rising, level or slowing, from the verification stamps.
KPIS.whyCompany: Pace of verified work, month on month, from recorded stamps.

KPIS.label: Profile coverage
KPIS.numerator: Required competencies of the selected work role or environment profile at verified or better.
KPIS.denominator: Required competencies the selected work role or environment profile names.
KPIS.whyMember: Measures the verified skills against a job role or a published company profile, with the untaught gap named.
KPIS.whyCompany: Coverage of the competencies a work role or an environment profile requires, read from verified steps.

KPIS.label: Values recalled
KPIS.numerator: Recall activities answered correctly: the value the team recorded, picked among distractors.
KPIS.denominator: Recall activities answered, from the checkpoints reached.
KPIS.whyMember: Weeks after recording an address, a prefix, a port or a decision, the member still knows it.
KPIS.whyCompany: Retention of the project the member built, read from answers given without the form open.

KPIS.label: Scenarios applied
KPIS.numerator: Applied scenarios answered correctly: an address inside the prefix, a free port on the host, the committed size.
KPIS.denominator: Applied scenarios offered at the checkpoints reached.
KPIS.whyMember: Takes a value the team recorded and uses it under a change the course did not script.
KPIS.whyCompany: Applied use of recorded facts, not recall alone; offered scenarios count whether or not answered.

KPIS.label: Conflicts resolved
KPIS.numerator: Conflicts the record found that the team resolved: the address, the port, the prefix, the size no longer at odds.
KPIS.denominator: Conflicts the record found at the checkpoints reached, resolved or still open.
KPIS.whyMember: A duplicate address or an over-committed host found by the platform and fixed by the team.
KPIS.whyCompany: Contradictions in the record closed, read from the record itself rather than from a claim.

KPIS.label: Minutes on task
KPIS.numerator: Whole minutes the member had tasks of this course open on a visible tab, pauses excluded.
KPIS.denominator: A count; nothing is read into it.
KPIS.whyMember: How long the work took the member, by the timer they can pause; measured, never rewarded.
KPIS.whyCompany: Time on task as context for the other rows; no score reads it.

PRACTICES.label: Least privilege
PRACTICES.definition: Every account, role and agent holds only the rights its task needs, and nothing it might need later.

PRACTICES.label: Defence in depth
PRACTICES.definition: More than one control stands between an attacker and the asset, so one failure is not a breach.

PRACTICES.label: Default deny
PRACTICES.definition: Nothing passes a boundary unless a rule allows it; the allow list is the policy.

PRACTICES.label: Network segmentation
PRACTICES.definition: Zones with distinct trust levels are separated, and the flows between them are named and limited.

PRACTICES.label: Multi-factor authentication
PRACTICES.definition: Every console and privileged login asks for a second factor; a password alone is refused.

PRACTICES.label: Hash evidence at capture
PRACTICES.definition: Every artifact is hashed when it is saved and the digest is recorded, so later copies can be checked.

PRACTICES.label: Authorised testing only
PRACTICES.definition: Scanning and attacks happen inside a signed scope and rules of engagement, against the pod the team owns.

PRACTICES.label: Retest to closure
PRACTICES.definition: A finding is closed only by a retest that shows the fix, and every finding ends Closed, Open or Risk accepted.

PRACTICES.label: Change control
PRACTICES.definition: Every change is requested, reviewed, reversible and recorded before it reaches a system.

PRACTICES.label: Hardening baseline
PRACTICES.definition: Hosts are configured to a written benchmark and checked against it, so drift from the baseline is visible.

PRACTICES.label: Dependency and image scanning
PRACTICES.definition: Third-party packages and container images are scanned for known vulnerabilities before release.

PRACTICES.label: Guardrail regression tests
PRACTICES.definition: Every blocked attack case becomes a test the pipeline runs, so a removed guardrail fails the build.

PRACTICES.label: Budget guardrails
PRACTICES.definition: A budget with alerts is set before the first resource, and the alert is tested.

PRACTICES.label: Centralised logging
PRACTICES.definition: Every host ships its logs to one place where they are kept, searched and alerted on.

PRACTICES.label: Contain before analysing
PRACTICES.definition: An active attacker is blocked and the block is timestamped before the deeper analysis begins.

PRACTICES.label: Written runbooks
PRACTICES.definition: Routine operations are written as steps a colleague could follow, and the steps are kept current.

PRACTICES.label: As-built documentation
PRACTICES.definition: What was actually built is recorded, with addresses, versions and owners, and handed over with the system.

PRACTICES.label: Architecture decision records
PRACTICES.definition: Each significant design choice is recorded with its context, options and consequences.

PRACTICES.label: Data classification
PRACTICES.definition: Information is classified on a written scale, and handling rules follow the class.

PRACTICES.label: Control mapping
PRACTICES.definition: Each control is mapped to the criteria it satisfies across frameworks, with an owner and an evidence source.

PRACTICES.label: Corrective action
PRACTICES.definition: Every nonconformity gets a cause, a corrective action, an owner and a date, and the action is checked.

PRACTICES.label: Customer assurance
PRACTICES.definition: A customer question is answered with evidence or an honest gap, never with a promise.

PRACTICES.label: Input and output guardrails
PRACTICES.definition: Prompts and model outputs pass through filters that block or contain the listed attack cases.

PRACTICES.label: Human checkpoint
PRACTICES.definition: AI-assisted work passes a named human check before it is acted on, and the check is recorded.

PRACTICES.label: Suites with a pass line
PRACTICES.definition: An attack or evaluation suite states what passing means before it runs.

PRACTICES.label: Encryption at rest
PRACTICES.definition: Stored data, snapshots and backups are encrypted under a managed key, and nothing is shared or public.

PRACTICES.label: Redundant paths
PRACTICES.definition: A second link or device exists for every single point of failure, and the failover is tested by pulling the cable.

SCORING.label: Tool proficiency
SCORING.definition: Commands and skills proven by output, and skills proved on a second task, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Reads browser checks and receipts of stamps, not proof of the machine; the per-tool table names each command.

SCORING.label: Troubleshooting success
SCORING.definition: Faults resolved, retries that verified, stuck flags cleared and steps resolved within the hour, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Faults are team rows; the minutes are a median between two recorded stamps, so a step left open overnight is counted apart.

SCORING.label: Judgment
SCORING.definition: Decisions recorded, justified and approved, and changes with a rollback written, equally weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Counts what was written against named options; it does not judge whether the choice was right.

SCORING.label: Collaboration
SCORING.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected and peer reviews given, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Team facts count for the team; the role share on the KPIs says what this member moved.

SCORING.label: Reliability
SCORING.definition: On time against the cohort calendar, document control complete, controls cited and instructor approval, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: On time needs the cohort start date; without one the score stands on the other three and says so.

SCORING.label: Readiness
SCORING.definition: Exam weight verified, work-role coverage, skills retained and steps in order, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: A reading of the record against an exam and a work role, not a prediction of a pass or a hire.

SCORING.label: Understanding retained
SCORING.definition: Values recalled, scenarios applied and conflicts resolved, weeks after the team recorded them, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Asks only about values the team recorded; before the checkpoint week the score stands on nothing and says so.

SOPS.label: Incident response plan
SOPS.definition: The written plan for handling an incident: roles, the first hour, containment, communication and the notice deadline.

SOPS.label: Chain of custody
SOPS.definition: Every evidence item logged with its hash, who held it, when, and where it is stored.

SOPS.label: Hardening baseline
SOPS.definition: The settings a host must have, the benchmark they come from, and the proof each host meets them.

SOPS.label: Operational handover
SOPS.definition: What was built, how it is run, who owns it and what is still open, handed to the next team.

SOPS.label: Risk register
SOPS.definition: Each risk with its likelihood, impact, score, owner and treatment, reviewed on a schedule.

SOPS.label: Data handling standard
SOPS.definition: How data is classified, where it may live, how it is redacted and how media is sanitised.

SOPS.label: Monitoring plan
SOPS.definition: What is watched, from which sources, who is alerted, and what a page means.

SOPS.label: Asset inventory
SOPS.definition: Every asset with an owner, a location, a classification and its place in the picture.

SOPS.label: Control mapping
SOPS.definition: Each control mapped to the criteria it meets, with an owner and the evidence that proves it.

SOPS.label: Architecture record
SOPS.definition: The components, the trust boundaries, the flows and the decisions, with the reasons for each.

SOPS.label: Network design
SOPS.definition: Zones, allowed flows, the addressing plan and the default-deny statement.

SOPS.label: Pipeline record
SOPS.definition: The stages, the gates, what each blocks on, and the deployment that went through.

SOPS.label: Portfolio record
SOPS.definition: The repository, a case study, three resume bullets, the architecture diagram and the skills demonstrated, for one project.

STANDARDS.label: NIST CSF
STANDARDS.description: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
STANDARDS.why: Organises all security work into six functions. Tagging a step here shows which part of the lifecycle it strengthens and proves the work covered the whole picture, not just attack or defence.

STANDARDS.label: CIS
STANDARDS.description: CIS Critical Security Controls v8 and the CIS Benchmarks
STANDARDS.why: A prioritised "do these first" list of safeguards. A CIS tag means this step implements an industry-baseline control that auditors and blue teams recognise at once.

STANDARDS.label: OWASP
STANDARDS.description: OWASP Top 10 and the Web Security Testing Guide
STANDARDS.why: Catalogues the most common web application weaknesses. This tag means the step attacks or defends one of those top risks, the shared language developers use to talk about web security.

STANDARDS.label: NIST 800-61
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-61 Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
STANDARDS.why: The incident-handling playbook: prepare, detect and analyse, contain, eradicate, recover, learn. This tag means the step is part of a defensible, court-ready incident response process.

STANDARDS.label: NIST 800-115
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-115 Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment
STANDARDS.why: The standard method for security testing and assessment. Following it makes scanning and exploitation repeatable, authorised and credible in a report.

STANDARDS.label: ISO 27001
STANDARDS.description: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 information security management system
STANDARDS.why: The certifiable information security management standard. This tag means the step produces the documented policy or evidence an ISO 27001 audit expects to see.

STANDARDS.label: SOC 2
STANDARDS.description: AICPA Trust Services Criteria for a SOC 2 examination
STANDARDS.why: The AICPA attestation standard built on the Trust Services Criteria: Security is CC1 to CC9, plus Availability, Confidentiality and the rest. This tag means the step produces a control or the evidence a SOC 2 Type I or II examiner samples.

STANDARDS.label: STRIDE
STANDARDS.description: STRIDE threat modelling
STANDARDS.why: A threat modelling lens: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. It names the category of threat this step addresses.

STANDARDS.label: ITIL 4
STANDARDS.description: ITIL 4 service management practices: change, incident, problem, release
STANDARDS.why: The operating disciplines a network team is judged on: change, incident and problem management. A tag here means the step is not just technically right but done the way an organisation can audit: requested, reviewed, reversible and recorded.

STANDARDS.label: Well-Architected
STANDARDS.description: Well-Architected Framework pillars, Azure and AWS
STANDARDS.why: Both clouds judge a design on the same pillars: reliability, security, cost, operational excellence and performance. A tag here means the step is a design choice one of them would ask about.

STANDARDS.label: NIST AI RMF
STANDARDS.description: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 and its Generative AI Profile
STANDARDS.why: The AI framework Ridgeline adopts: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. A tag here means the step produces something an AI risk register or the AI questions a buyer asks will ask for.

STANDARDS.label: OWASP LLM Top 10
STANDARDS.description: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications
STANDARDS.why: The shared catalogue of LLM application weaknesses: prompt injection, sensitive disclosure, excessive agency and the rest. A tag here names the weakness the step attacks or defends.

STANDARDS.label: MITRE ATLAS
STANDARDS.description: MITRE ATLAS: adversary tactics and techniques against AI systems
STANDARDS.why: ATT&CK for AI: real-world techniques attackers use against models and their data. Mapping a case to an ATLAS technique makes it comparable with the threat intelligence everyone else holds.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC 42001
STANDARDS.description: ISO/IEC 42001 AI management system
STANDARDS.why: The certifiable management system standard for AI. Customers ask about it; a tag here means the step produces the kind of record an AI management system keeps.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-53
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 security and privacy controls
STANDARDS.why: The federal control catalogue the sixteen CISSP control statements are drawn from (PM-1, SC-7, AC-2). A tag here means the step writes or proves one of those controls.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-30
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-30 Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments
STANDARDS.why: The federal method for a risk assessment: threat sources, events, likelihood and impact. A risk register that follows it can be defended line by line.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-88
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-88 Guidelines for Media Sanitization
STANDARDS.why: Clear, purge, destroy: the three sanitisation levels and when each applies. A disposal record that cites it proves the data left with the hardware.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-207
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture
STANDARDS.why: The reference for zero trust: no implicit trust from network location, every access decided per request. A network design that cites it explains its default-deny rules.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-63
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-63-4 Digital Identity Guidelines
STANDARDS.why: The assurance levels for identity proofing, authenticators and federation. An identity standard that cites it says which level MFA and single sign-on reach.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-218
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-218 Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)
STANDARDS.why: The practices a secure software pipeline follows: protect the code, produce well-secured software, respond to vulnerabilities. A pipeline record that cites it names the gate each practice became.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC 27005
STANDARDS.description: ISO/IEC 27005 information security risk management
STANDARDS.why: The risk method behind ISO 27001 clause 6: identify, analyse, evaluate, treat. A risk register that cites it reads the same way to an auditor.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC 27037
STANDARDS.description: ISO/IEC 27037 identification, collection, acquisition and preservation of digital evidence
STANDARDS.why: How evidence is collected and kept so it still counts later: identify, collect, acquire, preserve, with a chain of custody. An evidence log that cites it can be trusted in a dispute.

STANDARDS.why: What an architecture description must contain: stakeholders, concerns, viewpoints and the decisions behind them. A solution architecture document that cites it is complete rather than a diagram.

CUSTODY_RULES: Preserve the original — work on copies; never edit or rename the original artifact after collection.
Name every artifact `YYYYMMDD_TeamXX_Tool_Action.ext` so it is dated, attributed and self-describing.
Hash on collection: `sha256sum <file> >> Evidence_Hashes.txt`. Verify on receipt/before reporting: `sha256sum -c Evidence_Hashes.txt`.
Log every artifact in this file the moment it is collected — and log every hand-off (who → who, when).
Keep every artifact for a week in `~/team-artifacts/week-N/`; the team package gathers them into `04_Testing_and_Findings/Evidence/`. Keep originals read-only and backed up.
One custodian holds the evidence at a time; record each transfer so the chain is unbroken.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The terminal doesn’t recognise the program — usually a typo or the tool isn’t installed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the spelling. If it’s really missing, install it: sudo apt update && sudo apt install <tool>

variants.otherwise: — the step that first uses a tool says how to install it.

ERROR_ROWS.fix: Add sudo in front on Linux (sudo <command>). On Windows/PowerShell, close it and reopen with “Run as administrator”.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Connection refused / No route to host / host seems down
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You can’t reach the target — it’s off, the IP is wrong, or you’re not on the right network.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: ping the address first. Confirm the machine is powered on and that you are on the same subnet as it

variants.then: , and that you set the right IP in Lab access.
variants.otherwise: — a host in another zone only answers once the route between them exists.

variants.then: For nmap, add -Pn to scan a host that blocks ping.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You’re in the wrong folder, or the path/filename is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run pwd to see where you are and cd ~ to go home.

variants.then: For hydra, rockyou is gzipped by default — unzip it once: sudo gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz
variants.otherwise: Check the file really exists with ls before you edit it — a config path is easy to mistype.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: That’s a placeholder, not a real address — you copied it literally.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Open the Lab access panel at the top of the Tasks tab and enter {label}; the site then fills it into every command automatically.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: ssh: connect to host … Operation timed out (from home)
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Your laptop is not on the tailnet, or the host is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the Tailscale client is signed in and connected on your laptop, then run tailscale status on the host — it must list the host as online. On campus you can still reach it on its 10.10.30.T address while you sort this out.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: The Proxmox console times out but SSH works
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The path is fine; the web service or the port is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run systemctl status pveproxy --no-pager over SSH. Remember the console is on port 8006 and https, not http — a plain http:// URL simply hangs.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: It worked yesterday and not today
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The host rebooted and something did not come back, or your address changed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: systemctl is-active tailscaled on the host must read active. The host keeps the same Tailscale address across reboots, so if the address you saved has changed, you are looking at a rebuilt host that was re-authorised as a new device.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Permission denied (publickey) after setting up keys
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The key is not where the server expects it, or the account is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run ssh -v to see which key is offered, and confirm you are connecting as the right user. Password login is still enabled until Week 4 hardens it, so you have a way back in — use it rather than locking yourself out further.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The VM cannot reach the Core over the ops network — the second NIC, the VLAN tag or the bridge is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: On the host, ip -br a must show vmbr9 UP with the team’s 10.20.T.1 address. Inside the VM, the second interface needs its 10.20.T.x address and no gateway. Still nothing: the switch port is not trunking VLAN 20 — the Networking deep-dive owns that.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Some commands (a bare ping, a large download, a package install) run until you stop them, or they’re waiting on a slow or unreachable host.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Press Ctrl+C to stop it. Re-check reachability (ping), and give a genuinely long job a minute

variants.otherwise: — an OS install or a big apt upgrade takes minutes, not seconds.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: When anything fails, the error’s last line usually names the real problem.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Match that line to the rows above. Also double-check you’re on the machine the step’s WHERE chip names — running the right command on the wrong host is the most common cause.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Open a terminal
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: On a Linux desktop, click the black terminal icon or press Ctrl+Alt+T. On a server you reach over SSH, the terminal is the session itself. You type commands here and press Enter to run them.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: The prompt
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: A line ending in $ (or #) is the prompt — it means the terminal is waiting for you. You don’t type the $ itself.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Paste a command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Copy from this site, then in the terminal press Ctrl+Shift+V (plain Ctrl+V often does nothing in a terminal). Right-click → Paste also works.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Run one line at a time
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: When a step shows several numbered commands, run them one by one — paste one, press Enter, wait for it to finish, then the next.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: sudo = run as admin
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: sudo runs a command with admin rights (it may ask for your password — typing shows nothing, that’s normal). On Windows/PowerShell, instead right-click PowerShell → “Run as administrator”.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Stop a stuck command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Press Ctrl+C to cancel a command that hangs or runs forever (e.g. a ping with no -c limit).
